newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodians rejoice at report of Pol Pot surrender.
newsitem.headline: Cambodians rejoice at report of Pol Pot surrender.

text.p: Cambodians on Wednesday were delighted with news that Khmer Rouge guerrilla leader Pol Pot had surrendered to his former comrades and warned of revenge from the families of his many vicitms.

Clandestine Khmer Rouge radio, which is now apparently in the hands of a faction which broke with the reviled guerrilla commander earlier this month, reported on Wednesday that Pol Pot had turned himself in to them.
The radio gave no details as to his fate or whereabouts but political leaders in Phnom Penh said if the report were true, Pol Pot should be brought to the capital and put on trial.
Rumours of the ailing Pol Pot's whereabouts and even his death have flourished before.
More than one million Cambodians died during Pol Pot's 1975-79 rule. Many were worked to death or died of starvation while countless others were executed as enemies of his Maoist-style revolution.
Ordinary Cambodians said the demise of the shadowy Pol Pot could mean the end of long years of bitterness and war.
"I think this is the end of the anger of the people who suffered and whose families died during his rule," said one goverment worker who declined to be identified.
"If it's true, the Cambodian people will be really happy and when Pol Pot is arrested and brought to court we want to see his real face and hear his voice," he said.
The Khmer Rouge boycotted a 1993 election organised by the United Nations and have waged a guerrilla war against the government since then.
"This is good news because it means that we're close to the end of war but we must be careful. Pol Pot has many tricks," said local reporter Lor Chandara.
"If Pol Pot is taken to Phnom Penh many Cambodian people would demonstrate against him. Every Cambodian hates him so much," he said.
Others warned of a more violent reaction if Pol Pot were ever brought to the capital.
"If Pol Pot is brought to Phnom Penh he must be well protected or victims' families will take revenge," said civil servant Chay Sothy.

"The police won't be able to stop the people from attacking him. He can't come to Phnom Penh or he'll face torture," he said. "He should be detained in a secure place and let him die slowly, not so fast."
A motor cyle taxi driver said the memories of Pol Pot's "killing fields" rule would never fade.
"I'll never forget. It was terrible, a lot of people died and there was not enough food," said the man who identified himself as Visma.
"I want to see him in prison because he killed too many people," he said.
Pol Pot, who is now nearly 70 years old, was condemned to death in absentia by a Phnom Penh court soon after his government was overthrown by a Vietnamese invasion force in early 1979.
